predecessors.name: Byzantine Empire
predecessors.text: Bithynia and western Asia Minor: the Bithynian towns Theodore Laskaris secured 'in Alexios III's name until the end of 1204', Philadelphia (Mangaphas) and the Meander valley (Asidenos)

predecessors.name: Empire of Thessalonica
predecessors.text: Thessalonica and its environs, the Empire of Thessalonica

successors.name: Byzantine Empire
successors.text: the whole empire, which became the restored Byzantine Empire when Michael VIII entered Constantinople on 15 August 1261

ledger.x: Theodore 'secured the Bithynian towns' loyalty in Alexios III's name until the end of 1204' and 'established his seat in Bursa'; imperial title early 1205, Nicaea the capital from 1205, coronation 6 April 1208.
Poemanenum 6 December 1204, Adramyttion 19 March 1205: the Latins took the Bithynian and Mysian forts.
'Latins captured most of Bithynia by 1205'.
After Adrianople (14 April 1205) Theodore 'expelled the Latin garrisons from most Anatolian fortresses'.
'Mangaphas ceded Philadelphia to Theodore' and Asidenos' lands were absorbed (1205); independent Greek lords, stateless for the map.
'The Latins invaded Asia Minor and captured Nicomedia and Cyzicus during the winter of 1206-1207.'
Two-year truce of 1207: Theodore authorised 'to destroy two fortifications at Nicomedia and Cyzicus'.
Bithynia and Mysia

Alexios I of Trebizond page: 'In 1208 Theodore decided to strike against the Paphlagonian possessions of Alexios' brother David'; David Komnenos page: in 1208 Laskaris 'invested Heraclea Pontica' and lifted the siege when Henry of Flanders occupied Nicomedia.
Kaykhusraw I invaded with Alexios III; Antioch on the Meander 'probably 17 June 1211', 'Nicaean victory', the sultan killed.
Truce with Kaykaus I; the border 'would remain virtually unchallenged until the 1260s'.
Rhyndacus 15 October 1211; Henry marched to Nymphaion.
Nicaea lost 'most of Mysia and the Marmara Sea coast'; the Treaty of Nymphaeum gave the Latins 'most of [Mysia] up to the village of Kalamos'.

Battle of Antioch on the Meander page: 'in 1212, the death of David Komnenos allowed their annexation of his lands in Paphlagonia' (David died 13 December 1212, David Komnenos page); Theodore I Laskaris page: Theodore 'forced David Komnenos to abandon Heraclea Pontica on the Black Sea'.
Treaty of Nymphaeum (1214) page: 'Theodore was thus able to annex all of David's lands west of Sinope in late 1214'.

Matches empire-of-trebizond /ledger/9 (Empire of Trebizond page: 'the territories west of Sinope were lost to Theodore I Laskaris by 1214'); region widened on 2026-10-19 from 33.5E to 34.4E with the 1214 gain.
Treaty of Nymphaeum, December 1214 (or 1212 per Treadgold).
Poimanenon, early 1224 (or late 1223): Vatatzes crushed the Latin-backed Laskaris brothers.
1225 peace: Robert 'was forced to cede all his Asian possessions to Nicaea, except for Nicomedia'.
'Nicaea also took Aegean islands' (Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Ikaria, Kos) 1224-25; the Vatatzes page does not list them.
Vatatzes' 'seizure of Adrianople' after the 1225 concessions; the Empire of Thessalonica page: 'seized Adrianople from the Latins in 1225'.
the Latin lands in Asia under the Treaty of Nymphaeum: the Bithynian coast, Nicomedia, Pegai, Cyzicus, the Troad and Mysia to Kalamos
Theodore Komnenos Doukas 'drove the Nicaean garrison out of Adrianople and annexed much of Thrace in 1227'; the Epirus dossier dates the Epirote gain 1225.
Vatatzes 'launched an expedition against Rhodes in 1232/3'; the island was ravaged but Gabalas kept effective control.
Rhodes

Leo Gabalas 'acknowledged some form of suzerainty by the Empire of Nicaea' after the expedition (while treating with Venice in August 1234); John Gabalas held Nicaean titles (sebastos, megas doux) and 'was dependent on the Empire of Nicaea'.
Spring 1235.
'In 1235, finally, the last Latin possessions fell to Nicaea.'
Joint Bulgarian-Nicaean siege of Constantinople, 1235 - spring 1236, repulsed.
Constantinople and its environs
Ivan Asen II changed sides and 'attacked Nicaean holdings, including Tzurulum' (1237); Baldwin II held it 1240-1247 (not on the pages opened).

1242: John Komnenos Doukas 'was easily induced to content himself with the title of despotes and to recognize the suzerainty of Nicaea'; Vatatzes 'imposed his own suzerainty over Thessalonica (in 1242)'.
Annexed by Nicaea itself (December 1246).
'Thessalonica was incorporated into the Nicaean state' (1246), Demetrios Angelos Doukas deposed.
1246: John III annexes Thessalonica 'as well as much of Bulgarian Thrace in 1246' (John III Doukas Vatatzes page, after Ivan Asen II's death in 1241).
'By 1247, the Nicaeans had effectively surrounded the main holdings of the Emperor'; Tzurulum and Vizye taken 1247 (standard narrative, not on the pages opened).
'The Genoese took possession of the city and island, a dependency of the Empire of Nicaea, in a surprise attack in 1248'; John Kantakouzenos' expedition late 1248/early 1249; Achaean relief May 1249.
Genoese surrender 'either in late 1249 or early 1250'.
'After 1250, Gabalas family rule over Rhodes was terminated formally as well as de facto' - annexed by Nicaea itself.
'the island became a Nicaean province'; Vatatzes 'annexed the important island of Rhodes'.
Michael II's attack on Thessalonica (1251) and Vatatzes' counter-campaign of 1252.
'Michael's allies Golem of Kruja and Theodore Petraliphas defected to John III in 1252'; Michael II ceded Vodena, Kastoria and Deabolis (Epirus dossier: 'all his remaining holdings in Macedonia').
western Macedonia and Albania
Michael II Asen 'invaded Macedonia and Thrace in December 1254 or January 1255'.
'The Bulgarians quickly seized most Thracian fortresses'; 'Two Macedonian towns, Veles and Skopje, also surrendered to them.'
Theodore II's winter campaign 'forced the Bulgarian garrison in Veles to surrender' and his generals crossed the Rhodopes (1255).
Theodore II held Michael II's wife 'only allowing her to return to Epirus after Michael II ceded Servia and Dyrrachium to him' (1256), securing the Via Egnatia.
Treaty of 29 June 1256 'about the restoration of the prewar boundaries between Nicaea and Bulgaria'; Skopje back to Nicaea.
'The treaty prescribed that Michael II cede Tzepaina to the Nicaeans'; 'The Bulgarians ceded the fortress in early September' 1256.
Epirote-Nicaean conflict 1257-59: Michael II in alliance with Serbia and Manfred; 'Stefan Uros I defeated the Nicaean troops near Prilep'; Nicaean army 'routed at Edessa'.
'Palaiologos' withdrawal enabled Michael II to seize Prilep and capture Akropolites, who was its governor' (1257/58).
Manfred 'expelled the Nicaean garrisons from Dyrrachium and other fortresses on the Adriatic by the end of February 1258'.
Pelagonia (1259): Michael Palaiologos 'defeated a combined invasion by Manfred, the Despot of Epirus, and the Latin Prince of Achaea'; Prilep and Pelagonia recovered.
After Pelagonia the Nicaeans took Arta and overran Epirus and Thessaly (the Epirus dossier records the same occupation with the roles reversed); Michael II recovered his lands in spring 1260.

Battle of Pelagonia page: 'an anti-Nicaean alliance comprising Despotate of Epirus, Kingdom of Sicily and the Principality of Achaea'; infobox date 'Early summer or autumn of 1259' (no month; principality-of-achaea /ledger/15 has June).
Battle of Pelagonia page: many nobles 'including Villehardouin, were taken captive' and he was later 'released in exchange for three fortresses'.
Epirus and Thessaly, Michael II's domains
The conflict petered out with the Epirote recovery of 1260; the 'Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-59)' page would not load.
Siege of Galata 1260; Genoese alliance March 1261 (Treaty of Nymphaeum).
Alexios Strategopoulos' 800 men entered Constantinople on the night of 24/25 July 1261; Michael VIII entered 15 August.
Constantinople and its environs
The Empire of Nicaea becomes the restored Byzantine Empire (Palaiologos dynasty); rule 2 would allow a rename, but Cliopatria has separate rows and the byzantine-empire dossier is the sibling's.
Infobox: 'Disestablished: July 1261'.

wars.name: Latin-Nicaean war of 1204-1207
wars.outcome: Latin victories at Poimanenon and Adramyttion undone after Adrianople; Nicomedia and Cyzicus razed under the 1207 truce

wars.name: Nicaean-Trapezuntine war for Paphlagonia
wars.outcome: Heraclea and Amastris to Nicaea (1212), the rest of Paphlagonia west of Sinope (1214); Sinope to Rum (1 November 1214)

wars.name: Seljuk invasion of 1211
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory at Antioch on the Meander (c.

wars.name: Latin-Nicaean war of 1211-1214
wars.outcome: Latin victory at the Rhyndacus (15 October 1211); Treaty of Nymphaeum (December 1214)

wars.name: Poimanenon war
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory; all Latin Asia but Nicomedia ceded (1225); islands and Adrianople taken

wars.name: Nicaean expedition to Rhodes
wars.outcome: Island ravaged; Gabalas kept Rhodes under Nicaean suzerainty

wars.name: Siege of Constantinople (1235-1236)
wars.outcome: Siege repulsed; Nicaea kept Gallipoli and the Thracian coast

wars.name: Nicaean conquest of Thessalonica and Macedonia (1246)
wars.outcome: Thessalonica annexed; Serres, Melnik, Skopje, Veles, Prosek and Thrace to Stenimachos taken from Bulgaria

wars.name: Genoese occupation of Rhodes
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory; Rhodes a Nicaean province

wars.name: Bulgarian-Nicaean war of 1254-1256
wars.outcome: Treaty of 29 June 1256 restoring the prewar boundaries; Tzepaina ceded to Nicaea (September 1256)

wars.name: Epirote-Nicaean conflict (1257-1259)
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory at Pelagonia (1259) and occupation of Epirus; Michael II recovered Epirus in 1260; Manfred kept the Adriatic towns

wars.name: Reconquest of Constantinople
wars.outcome: Nicaean victory 25 July 1261; the Byzantine Empire restored

certainty.note: The Seljuk frontier was stable after 1211; the Latin, Trapezuntine, Bulgarian and Epirote frontiers moved with each campaign and are dated by single pages.
